clue.text: Emma is hurt after handling complaint

indicators.note: something that has been handled has been pushed about and reworked, so these letters come out in a new order

explanation.surface: Poor Emma is in pain after picking something up, and grumbles about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hurt' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder: EMMA IS HURT, rearranged as signalled by 'after handling', gives the ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is an ailment, and this painful condition of the joints and muscles is a classic example.

clue.text: Local outlet initially lacking place to keep stock

indicators.note: the word for the outlet goes without its opening letter, which is what initially lacking asks for

parts.note: a local shop belonging to a chain is one of its branches

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood shop has nowhere to store its goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stock' suggests shop goods, but here it means livestock: cattle are kept on the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock in the farming sense is cattle, and a large farm for rearing them is the place they are kept.

clue.text: Televised sport English doctor starts receiving

indicators.note: the English doctor starts off the answer, coming in front of the sport though the clue names it later

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
horse racing is a sport often shown on television

explanation.surface: An English physician begins to pick up a televised sports broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' is positional: the English doctor begins the answer even though the clue names the sport first.
explanation.definitionFit: To receive someone warmly is to welcome them with open arms, which is the same as holding them close in a hug.

clue.text: Fighting force?

parts.note: reads as an army unit, but the force is a police body whose job is to deal with soldiers, including those who are fighting

explanation.definitionFit: These are the officers who enforce discipline within the army, a police force for soldiers.

clue.text: Engine starts to rev better in air, going round

indicators.note: the word for the air surrounds the three opening letters, going round them

parts.note: an air is a tune or melody

indicators.note: only the opening letters of rev, better and in are taken

explanation.surface: Mechanical advice: rev a motor harder while it is airborne and turning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes R, B and I from 'rev better in'; 'going round' puts TUNE around them.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotary machine driven by gas, steam or water is a type of engine, used in jets and power stations.

clue.text: Spot where moose and mushrooms have turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the whole run of letters is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the moose is called an elk in Europe
ceps are a kind of edible mushroom (porcini)

explanation.surface: A woodland scene where a moose and some mushrooms have appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'appeared', but in this down clue it turns ELK + CEPS upside down, giving SPECKLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A small mark or fleck of colour is a spot, as on an egg or a bird's feathers.

clue.text: Fine parade assembled for show

definitions.meaning: fine weather is pleasant and dry
a trade exhibition or show where goods are lined up for display

explanation.definitionFit: The word means pleasant or acceptable (fine), and also an exhibition where wares are put on display, as at a trade show.

clue.text: Excuse offered by politician overwhelmed by sloth

indicators.note: the sloth surrounds and swamps the politician, so the politician goes inside

parts.note: the ai is a three-toed sloth, a crossword favourite
Lib is short for a Liberal politician

explanation.surface: A lazy politician makes excuses while bogged down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sloth' reads as laziness, but it is the animal: AI, a three-toed sloth, holds LIB.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea that one was elsewhere when the deed was done is the standard excuse offered by a suspect.

clue.text: Title match won by visitors in short order

parts.note: a title to something is a legal right to it
a game won by the visiting team is an away win, or simply an away

explanation.surface: A championship belt goes to the touring team in a quick decision.
explanation.walkthrough: On British football pools coupons, a match won by the visiting side is marked as an away.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something immediately is to do it in short order, without delay.

clue.text: Top legal type from Cornell, endlessly cold and hard when busy

indicators.note: busy letters are bustling about, so the combined letters are rearranged
the word cold loses its final letter, which is what endlessly asks of it

explanation.surface: A leading lawyer hailing from Cornell University is chilly and tough when under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the D off COLD, giving COL; then 'when busy' shuffles CORNELL + COL + HARD into the answer. 'Cornell' looks like the American university but is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer of state was historically head of the judiciary in England and Wales, the most senior legal post.

clue.text: Cloud's curiously unreal, with black lining

indicators.note: black lines the inside of the rearranged word, so it goes within it
curiously signals the letters of unreal should be arranged in an odd new way

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a cloud with a dark edge looks strangely unreal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with black lining' puts B inside NEULAR, the anagram of UNREAL made by 'curiously'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to a nebula, an interstellar cloud of gas and dust, so it means of a cloud.

clue.text: Suggesting one's given out? That's about right

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, around, the word for right
out signals that the letters of given are put out of their usual order

parts.note: OK means all right, correct

explanation.surface: Someone hints that they have handed something out, and is told that is about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' shuffles the clue word given, and 'about' wraps the result around the word for right; 'one's' and 'That's' only join the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke something is to call it to mind, which is to bring it up as a suggestion or hint.

clue.text: Despondent rustic getting to grips with English literature etc

indicators.note: the rustic grips the other pieces, holding them inside

parts.note: a hick is an unsophisticated country person
literature and similar subjects are the arts

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin is down in the dumps trying to study English literature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting to grips with' means the countryman holds the English literature inside him; 'etc' widens literature to the arts in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sick at heart means being deeply unhappy, the same as despondent or dejected.

clue.text: Accumulation of snow brought fir down over here? Not entirely

indicators.note: over signals a turnover, the run of letters read backwards
only part of the words brought fir down is used, a run spanning them

explanation.surface: A storm has blown a fir tree down near here, though not all the way.
explanation.walkthrough: TFIRD runs through 'brough(T FIR D)own'; 'over' reads it backwards. 'here' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow piled up by the wind into a bank is a snowdrift, an accumulation of snow.

clue.text: Originator of 'the word on the street'?

definitions.text: Originator of 'the word on the street'?

parts.words: Originator of 'the word on the street'?
parts.note: the word on the street is gossip, but read literally it is a proclamation shouted aloud in the street by a town official ringing a bell

explanation.definitionFit: A town official who made public announcements in the streets was the source of news heard there.

clue.text: Not like registered unions?

parts.note: unions here are marriages rather than trade unions; a couple living together without registering a marriage are in this kind of partnership

explanation.definitionFit: A partnership of this kind is one recognised by custom rather than by a registered ceremony.

clue.text: Observer colour supplement?

parts.note: the Observer newspaper has a colour magazine, but an observer is also an eye, and makeup adds colour to the eyelid

explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper with a colour magazine supplement.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic colour brushed on the eyelids is makeup that supplements the colour around the organ of sight.

clue.text: Ties fated to dissolve? That's pessimistic

indicators.note: a thing that dissolves breaks up, so the letters break up and re-form

explanation.surface: Someone gloomily predicts that their relationships are doomed to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissolve' suits the doomed ties of the surface but is the anagram signal for TIES FATED.
explanation.definitionFit: A person expecting to lose and giving up in advance shows a gloomy outlook, the attitude of the pessimist.

clue.text: Handled volume booster

parts.note: volume might suggest a book, but this is sound volume, boosted by a cone-shaped device carried by a handle

explanation.definitionFit: A hand-held horn that amplifies the voice is a device with a handle for making sound louder.

clue.text: Far-off region in which a canoe's navigated round islands

indicators.note: the rearranged canoe goes round the letter for islands
the letters of a canoe are steered into a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written
I or Is is the abbreviation for island or islands on maps

explanation.surface: A distant part of the world where someone paddles a canoe around the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'navigated' rearranges A CANOE, and 'round' puts it around I for islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific islands and Australasia form a distant region of the globe as seen from Britain.

clue.text: Hard to find English, as it happens, going round America

indicators.note: the word for as it happens goes around the letters for America

parts.note: a live broadcast is shown as it happens
US is short for United States, America

explanation.surface: An Englishman travelling round the States finds things difficult to locate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it happens' looks like a throwaway phrase, but it means a broadcast shown in real time, which 'going round' wraps about America.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evasive or slippery is hard to catch or pin down, difficult to locate.

clue.text: Fine for one newspaper in New York

indicators.note: the one and newspaper go inside the letters for New York

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
the FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper in New York is fined.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT (Financial Times) is a British daily; 'in' puts it, after the numeral for one, inside the city's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart, neat or excellent, as in a clever gadget, means much the same as fine.

clue.text: Waste extracted from river

parts.note: of can mean from, as in coming of good family
the Fal is a river in Cornwall

explanation.surface: Rubbish is pulled out of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The FAL is a river in Cornwall, south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The entrails and organs removed from a slaughtered animal are discarded parts, though some are eaten.

clue.text: Cricket team in brilliant clothing turned up as arranged

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the slang word for brilliant clothes the team, holding it inside

parts.note: def is slang for excellent or brilliant
a cricket team is an eleven, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A cricket side in dazzling kit arrived just as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'arrived', but in this down clue it reverses the whole: the team inside the slang word for brilliant, read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something settled or set in advance has been arranged, as with a match that has been rigged.

clue.text: Axe Bunter characters going wild with elation?

indicators.note: the characters (letters) of the words run wild into a new order

explanation.surface: Billy Bunter is overjoyed at wielding an axe.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a greedy schoolboy from British children's stories. Here 'characters' means letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Overflowing with joy and enthusiasm, a person is full of high spirits.

clue.text: Gossip, taking time over drinks

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letter for time sits over the drinks, placed above them

parts.note: ales are beers

explanation.surface: Someone spreads rumours while taking their time over a few beers.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above: T on top of ALES.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip is idle talk, and telling stories about others is spreading rumours.

clue.text: In France the team study a dictionary

parts.note: le is French for the
a team of eleven players, XI in Roman numerals
to con is to study or learn by heart

explanation.surface: A French football team studies a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'study' is the old verb CON, to pore over.
explanation.definitionFit: A word list with meanings, especially for a language or specialised field, is a book of words.

clue.text: Malice one's shown with document

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Malice one's shown with document (3-4)': WILL is the document, but no reading of 'one's shown' gives ILL (it suits I'LL, 'one will', not 'one's'); likely an OCR or print slip that neither search nor scan resolves.

clue.text: Extra large

definitions.meaning: in cricket a ... is a delivery out of the batsman's reach, scored as a run not off the bat

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, extras are runs not scored off the bat; a ball bowled too far from the batsman is one.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a ball bowled out of reach scores a run as an extra, and broad means large across.

clue.text: Local drink prices?

parts.note: a local is a pub, suggesting beer prices, but read as local council charges they are bills for supplying a plain drink from the tap

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'local' is a neighbourhood pub; water supply charges were long levied by local bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: These are charges for a household's mains supply, the cost of the plainest drink, billed locally.
